contexts.title: Abortion coverage rules in Marketplace plans
contexts.html: KFF reports that “twelve states now have laws that require all fully-insured group plans and individual plans (including Marketplace plans) to include abortion coverage.” [44] Beyond the federal exceptions for rape, incest and danger to the pregnant person’s life, “this coverage cannot be paid with federal dollars.” [1] Plans must “Collect from each enrollee” [2] a separate payment for it: “May not estimate such a cost at less than one dollar per enrollee, per month.” [2] The larger credits lower the price of the whole plan for eligible buyers.

nodes.title: More people insured
nodes.claim_html: Compared with the law in force on January 8, 2026, the bill would increase the number of people with health insurance, mainly in 2027 and 2028.

nodes.title: Newly insured people use more care
nodes.claim_html: People who gain insurance because of the bill would face fewer cost barriers to medical care and would use more of it, including primary care, prescriptions and hospital care.

nodes.title: Added care adds energy, supply and waste demand
nodes.claim_html: By supporting more treatment and prescriptions, the bill would add some demand for the energy, manufactured supplies and waste handling that medical care uses. This is a claim about the added, marginal effect of the added care.

nodes.title: Added climate pollution
nodes.claim_html: The added care would add some greenhouse gases that warm the planet, adding to the threat that warming poses to habitats and species.

nodes.title: Added acid-forming pollution
nodes.claim_html: The added care would add some acid-forming pollution, mainly through electricity use by facilities and suppliers, adding harm to water life and plants.

nodes.title: Added smog-forming pollution
nodes.claim_html: The added care would add some pollution that forms ground-level ozone, adding to damage to trees and forests.

nodes.title: Added nutrient pollution
nodes.claim_html: The added care would add some nutrient (nitrogen) pollution, adding to damage to aquatic habitats and to changes in which plants grow.

nodes.title: Added drug pollution
nodes.claim_html: The added prescriptions would add some drug residues to waterways, from patients’ body waste, improper disposal and manufacturing, adding to harm to wild species.

nodes.title: Added toxic chemical pollution
nodes.claim_html: The added care would add some toxic chemical pollution and hazardous waste, mainly through waste handling, adding to threats to waters and wildlife.

nodes.title: Added lasting plastic waste
nodes.claim_html: The added care would add some lasting plastic waste from disposable supplies, adding to the risk to natural habitats.

nodes.title: Added water demand
nodes.claim_html: The added care would add some demand for water in facilities and supply chains, adding pressure on freshwater habitats where water is scarce.

nodes.title: Added mining demand
nodes.claim_html: The added demand for medical goods and energy would add some pressure to mine, which disturbs habitats.

nodes.title: Added ozone-layer risk from nitrous oxide
nodes.claim_html: The added hospital care would add some use and release of nitrous oxide, a pain-blocking gas that damages the ozone layer, adding risk to aquatic food webs.

nodes.title: Nature: pollution and resource demand from added care
nodes.claim_html: Greenhouse gases, acid, smog, nutrient and drug pollution, toxic and plastic waste, water and mining demand, and ozone-layer damage each threaten habitats, species or clean water. Adding to any of them works against protecting nature from destruction and pollution. Each kind needs its own claim; any one accepted claim is enough.

nodes.title: Farm families helped to stay on the land
nodes.claim_html: Lower premiums would help some farm families and farm workers who buy Marketplace coverage stay on their farms, rather than leave farming or sell the farm because of insurance costs.

nodes.title: Conservation farming continues
nodes.claim_html: Among the farms helped to stay in business, some are organic farms whose required plans protect soil, water and wildlife, so that conservation farming would continue.

nodes.title: Nature: work that protects nature kept going
nodes.claim_html: Organic farms that use fewer pesticides and care for soil, water and wildlife, businesses that offer less polluting energy such as solar, and habitat care and conservation volunteering each protect the natural environment. Helping such work continue, or lowering a personal cost of doing it, serves caring for nature. Each kind needs its own claim; any one accepted claim is enough.

nodes.title: Clean-energy businesses kept going
nodes.claim_html: Lower premiums would help some owners of businesses that offer less polluting energy, such as solar, keep that business going.

nodes.title: Lower personal cost of nature work
nodes.claim_html: Some people who take paid seasonal habitat jobs without insurance, or who volunteer for conservation work at their own medical risk, are eligible for the credits and buy Marketplace coverage. For them, the bill would lower a personal cost of that work.

nodes.title: Avoided pollution from kidney failure
nodes.claim_html: Some people who gain insurance because of the bill would get SGLT2 medicines that prevent hospital stays and kidney failure, lowering the total pollution from their care.

nodes.title: Avoided extra driving pollution
nodes.claim_html: By reducing the risk that local health services close, the bill would avoid some longer journeys to care and their climate pollution.

nodes.title: Nature: pollution avoided by keeping care
nodes.claim_html: Avoiding climate pollution, whether from kidney failure and hospital stays or from extra driving to distant care, serves protecting the environment. Each route needs its own claim; either is enough.

nodes.title: Less pressure to cut local health services
nodes.claim_html: Keeping more people insured would support provider revenue and limit unpaid care, reducing one source of pressure on hospitals and clinics to cut services.

nodes.title: Health-care jobs and local revenue protected
nodes.claim_html: By supporting provider revenue, the bill would protect some health-care jobs and pay, and some state and local tax revenue for public services, that would otherwise be lost.

nodes.title: Net national gain from protected health-care jobs and revenue
nodes.claim_html: Those protected health-care jobs, pay and public revenue would add, on net, to economic stability across the country, and not only support a particular flow of spending.

nodes.title: Concern: care for people who would otherwise go without
nodes.claim_html: People who go without needed care, whether because they lack insurance or because treatment bills are too high, live sicker lives. Bringing care within reach of people with little money and substantial health needs protects the vulnerable, and good health is a basis for equal opportunity in work and study. This can come through new coverage or through plans with lower treatment bills; each needs its own claim, and either is enough.

nodes.title: Easier replacement coverage after job loss
nodes.claim_html: The larger credits would make it easier for some people who lose job-based insurance to replace it with affordable coverage.

nodes.title: Concern: protection from medical bills
nodes.claim_html: Insurance protects people from financial hardship caused by medical bills, including people who lose a job, live where public insurance rules are narrow, or cannot reach veterans’ care. Protecting them serves protecting the vulnerable. This can come through more people insured or through easier replacement coverage after job loss; either is enough.

nodes.title: Concern: money left for basic needs
nodes.claim_html: Lower insurance payments leave more of a small budget for food, housing and other basic needs. Protecting financially vulnerable people from those sacrifices serves protecting the vulnerable.

nodes.title: Plans with lower treatment bills chosen
nodes.claim_html: The larger credits would lead some people to choose plans that charge less when they get care, lowering a cost barrier to needed treatment.

nodes.title: Smaller racial gaps in coverage
nodes.claim_html: The coverage the bill adds would go disproportionately to Black and Latino people, keeping racial gaps in insurance from widening.

nodes.title: Concern: racial gaps in coverage
nodes.claim_html: Keeping coverage losses from widening racial gaps in insurance serves equal opportunity and just treatment.

nodes.title: Concern: unequal earnings and the cost of coverage
nodes.claim_html: Help with insurance costs reduces the effect of pay discrimination and low-paid work on access to care. More equal access for people facing these disadvantages serves equal opportunity and just treatment.

nodes.title: Concern: help tied to income and insurance costs
nodes.claim_html: Help that phases out with income, rather than ending suddenly, protects people facing high bills because of age or location, treats people with nearly identical incomes more equally, and spares households a sudden repayment bill for barely crossing the line. That serves fair treatment.

nodes.title: Concern: fairer help across kinds of work
nodes.claim_html: Restoring help above the cutoff reduces the disadvantage of having to buy insurance yourself while job-based coverage receives tax help. Fairer access to public support across kinds of work serves just treatment.

nodes.title: More Marketplace enrollment
nodes.claim_html: The bill would increase enrollment through the Marketplaces, by about 6.2 million people in 2028.

nodes.title: Lower full insurance prices
nodes.claim_html: Healthier enrollment would lower the full, pre-credit prices of benchmark Marketplace plans in 2027–2029, helping buyers who get no credit.

nodes.title: Less risk of lost plan choices
nodes.claim_html: A larger Marketplace would give insurers more reason to compete and keep offering plans, reducing the risk that an insurer’s exit disrupts people’s coverage.

nodes.title: Concern: other buyers’ access to coverage
nodes.claim_html: Lower full prices, or a market less exposed to insurer exits, reduce barriers to coverage for other buyers, including people with no credit. Either is enough; each needs its own claim. That serves protecting people who rely on this market.

nodes.title: Concern: local health services kept
nodes.claim_html: Local services protect patients outside the Marketplaces too: “Community health centers serve people regardless of their ability to pay” [24]. Reducing pressure to cut them protects vulnerable patients.

nodes.title: Concern: health-care jobs and public services
nodes.claim_html: Protecting health-care workers’ jobs and pay, and the local revenue behind services such as education, protects households from hardship and keeps opportunities open.

nodes.title: Concern: aid above need while the poorest stay excluded
nodes.claim_html: Protecting the weakest and giving everyone equal opportunities means putting basic protection for those without it ahead of extra aid for people far above poverty. Adding aid for a small high-income group while the poorest uninsured remain excluded enlarges an unfair gap.

nodes.title: Added risk of unauthorized enrollment
nodes.claim_html: Under the rules in force on January 8, 2026, restoring the larger credits would add to the risk of Marketplace enrollment or plan changes made without a person’s knowledge or based on false information, by making plans with no monthly premium more widely available and by enlarging the payments involved.

nodes.title: Concern: vulnerable people exposed to broker abuse
nodes.claim_html: People who depend on steady care and cannot absorb unexpected debts are among the vulnerable. Added exposure to enrollment abuse that stops treatment or creates debts works against protecting them.

nodes.title: Concern: larger possible debts for victims
nodes.claim_html: A larger tax bill for a victim of an uncorrected false enrollment falls on people least able to absorb it. Raising that possible debt works against protecting the vulnerable.

nodes.title: Fewer people with job-based coverage
nodes.claim_html: The bill would lead to fewer people with job-based insurance, about 2.1 million fewer in 2028, mainly because some employers would stop offering it.

nodes.title: Covered access to a doctor lost
nodes.claim_html: Some people moving from job-based insurance to a Marketplace plan because of the bill would not find a plan that includes their doctor, and some of them would delay or miss needed care or pay more.

nodes.title: Concern: sick patients’ care and finances
nodes.claim_html: Losing covered access to a treating doctor, or paying more to keep that doctor, burdens sick patients. Protecting their care and finances gives a reason against that risk.

nodes.title: Added federal debt
nodes.claim_html: The bill would add about $80.6 billion to federal deficits over 2026–2035, which means more federal borrowing.

nodes.title: Added pressure on emergency borrowing
nodes.claim_html: The added debt would add a small amount to the budget pressure that CBO says might make lawmakers less willing to borrow to respond to unforeseen events, such as downturns or crises.

nodes.title: Concern: people who would bear the costs of added debt
nodes.claim_html: Harms from added federal debt can fall on people who become vulnerable: emergency aid for people who lose work or cannot afford food becoming harder to fund, lower future pay that makes it harder for workers to build secure lives, or a financial crisis that spreads abroad and threatens savings and livelihoods, including those of strangers in other countries. Concern for them gives a reason against adding to such a risk. Each harm needs its own claim; any one accepted claim is enough.

nodes.title: Less private investment
nodes.claim_html: The added borrowing would add a small amount to the reduction in private investment that CBO links to slower growth and lower worker pay over time.

nodes.title: Added fiscal-crisis risk
nodes.claim_html: The added debt would add a small amount to the risk of a fiscal crisis that CBO links to debt growing faster than the economy, a crisis that could spread to other countries.

nodes.title: Concern: protection of unborn children
nodes.claim_html: If unborn children are counted among the vulnerable, helping people buy plans that cover procedures ending developing human lives gives a reason, out of concern for those lives, to oppose the bill.

nodes.title: Tolerance: room for reproductive choices one may reject
nodes.claim_html: Accepting people despite disagreement gives a reason to support their coverage while leaving room for reproductive choices one may reject.

nodes.title: Health-center language and cultural services sustained
nodes.claim_html: By protecting health centers’ insurance income, the bill would help sustain services that let patients explain their needs across language and cultural differences.

nodes.title: Tolerance: listening across language and culture
nodes.claim_html: Helping patients explain their needs across language and cultural differences, and shape their own care, serves listening to and understanding people unlike oneself.

nodes.title: Tolerance: a higher cost for refusing the abortion payment
nodes.claim_html: Accepting people who disagree includes respecting their refusal to take part in a practice that violates their faith. Increasing the financial cost of that refusal works against that acceptance.

nodes.title: Religiously exempt job plans lost
nodes.claim_html: Some workers in religiously exempt job plans would lose that coverage because of the bill and would need a Marketplace plan that requires the abortion payment.

nodes.title: Tolerance: objecting workers pushed into the abortion payment
nodes.claim_html: Respecting people’s refusal to fund a practice that violates their faith gives a reason against pushing workers out of plans that honored that refusal.

nodes.title: Tolerance: public financing religious taxpayers reject
nodes.claim_html: Tolerance gives a reason to respect the limits people place on their own participation in a disputed practice, even when one disagrees. Expanding the public financing these taxpayers reject works against that respect.

nodes.title: Tolerance: room for religious health sharing
nodes.claim_html: Accepting different religious groups includes making room for how they practice their faith. A larger financial reason to replace that practice puts pressure on that acceptance.

nodes.title: Job coverage of religiously required care lost
nodes.claim_html: Some workers whose job plans cover abortions that some Jewish teaching requires to protect health would lose that coverage because of the bill and move to Marketplace plans that exclude it.

nodes.title: Tolerance: following Jewish teaching on health-protecting care
nodes.claim_html: Respecting a different faith includes respecting its members’ ability to follow its teachings when they need care.

nodes.title: Job coverage of transition care lost
nodes.claim_html: Some transgender workers whose job plans cover transition care would lose that coverage because of the bill and move to Marketplace plans that exclude it.

nodes.title: Tolerance: transgender workers’ care
nodes.claim_html: Accepting transgender people includes making room for them to live according to their gender identity. Losing coverage for care that supports that identity works against that acceptance.

nodes.title: Personal Security: needed care within reach
nodes.claim_html: For an average American who needs Marketplace coverage, now or after a change in work or family, care within reach brings prevention, medicines and treatment that protect physical and mental health and avoid danger to life. This can come through new coverage or through plans with lower treatment bills; each needs its own claim, and either is enough.

nodes.title: Less hardship over food, heat and housing
nodes.claim_html: Lower premiums would leave some Marketplace buyers enough money to avoid cutting back on food, heat or housing, reducing hardships linked to poor health.

nodes.title: Personal Security: health protected from financial strain
nodes.claim_html: Less financial strain protects health: keeping food on the table, heat and a safe home protects health and personal safety, and less harmful distress protects mental health. Each needs its own claim; either is enough.

nodes.title: Less financial distress
nodes.claim_html: Lower premiums would ease financial distress enough to protect the mental health of some Marketplace buyers, including people already insured.

nodes.title: Personal Security: coverage kept through changes in work or income
nodes.claim_html: A stronger option after losing a job, or help that no longer ends suddenly at the income line along with the large tax bill a small raise can trigger, reduces threats to keeping affordable coverage and continuing treatment through ordinary changes in work or income. The job-loss reason needs its own claim; the income-line reason rests on the bill’s rule. Either is enough.

nodes.title: Personal Security: coverage that is easier to buy and keep
nodes.claim_html: For an average American buying Marketplace coverage, lower full prices for buyers without a credit, or less risk of losing a plan that works for them, make health protection easier to buy and more dependable. Each needs its own claim; either is enough.

nodes.title: Personal Security: hospitals and clinics for everyone
nodes.claim_html: Hospitals and clinics also serve people insured through work or Medicare. Less pressure to cut their services protects everyone’s access to needed care.

nodes.title: Personal Security: care interrupted by unwanted plan changes
nodes.claim_html: Unwanted coverage changes can interrupt access to a doctor or medicine. Avoiding such interruptions protects health.

nodes.title: Personal Security: needed care lost after leaving job plans
nodes.claim_html: Going without needed care, whether from losing an established doctor, skipping useful care because treatment costs more, or going without dental care, works against protecting health and avoiding disease. Each needs its own claim; any one accepted claim is enough.

nodes.title: Higher treatment costs after leaving job plans
nodes.claim_html: Some people moving from job-based insurance to Marketplace plans because of the bill would pay a larger share of their treatment costs, and some would skip useful care as a result.

nodes.title: Lost dental protection
nodes.claim_html: Some people leaving job-based coverage because of the bill would lose employer dental benefits and face a separate unsubsidized bill to keep dental protection, so some would go without dental care.

nodes.title: Stronger control of contagious disease
nodes.claim_html: By reducing cost barriers to diagnosis and care for newly insured people, the bill would strengthen the country’s control of contagious disease outbreaks.

nodes.title: Societal Security: protection against disease, disasters and drug threats
nodes.claim_html: Better control of contagious disease, hospital capacity to respond to disasters and attacks, and a stronger response to a deadly drug threat each protect people beyond those receiving the credits and strengthen the country’s protection against threats. Each needs its own claim; any one accepted claim is enough.

nodes.title: Hospital disaster capacity preserved
nodes.claim_html: By easing financial pressure on hospitals, the bill would help preserve hospital services that emergency responders need during disasters and attacks.

nodes.title: Stronger response to the opioid crisis
nodes.claim_html: More affordable coverage would help some people with opioid addiction reach treatment, strengthening the country’s response to the opioid crisis.

nodes.title: Workforce kept healthier
nodes.claim_html: Care that prevents and manages illness among newly insured people would help preserve their ability to work enough to add to the country’s capacity to produce goods and provide services.

nodes.title: Societal Security: a stable national economy
nodes.claim_html: A workforce better able to produce goods and services, net national gains from protected health-care jobs and revenue, household spending that adds to national stability, and health protection kept through job losses in a downturn can each add to the country’s economic stability. A steadier economy supports a secure and stable country. Each needs its own claim; any one accepted claim is enough.

nodes.title: Household spending supports economic stability
nodes.claim_html: Money that lower premiums leave in policyholders’ budgets would support spending at other businesses enough to add to economic stability across the country.

nodes.title: Less pressure on state budgets
nodes.claim_html: Restored federal help would reduce pressure on states to divert limited funds to replace it, leaving those funds for other needs.

nodes.title: Societal Security: a capable state
nodes.claim_html: States able to use limited health funds for other needs are better able to protect their residents.

nodes.title: Health protection kept through downturns
nodes.claim_html: A more affordable route to coverage outside work would help the country absorb job losses in a downturn without losing as much health protection. This can come through easier replacement coverage after job loss or through lower full insurance prices; either is enough.

nodes.title: Societal Security: national strength and stability under added debt
nodes.claim_html: Added federal debt can weaken a secure country: added pressure against borrowing for defense and crisis response, a small added risk of financial breakdown, a risk to the stable funding and financial tools behind U.S. influence, pressure on the investment and growth that sustain national defense, or national income lost to interest paid abroad. Each needs its own claim; any one accepted claim is enough.

nodes.title: Weaker financial tools of U.S. influence
nodes.claim_html: The added debt would add a small amount to the risk of a gradual decline in the value of U.S. government bonds, making public activity harder to finance and weakening financial tools the United States uses to protect its interests.

nodes.title: Interest paid abroad
nodes.claim_html: The added debt would raise interest payments to foreign holders of U.S. debt, slightly lowering national income.

nodes.title: Societal Security: organized enrollment fraud
nodes.claim_html: A strong state must keep public resources from financing crime and protect citizens, through a reliable national insurance system, from organized abuse that can interrupt care. Added exposure to organized or hidden unauthorized enrollment works against both.

nodes.title: Societal Security: more public money within reach of fraud
nodes.claim_html: Larger payments per enrollment put more public money within reach of fraud schemes. Keeping public resources from financing crime gives a reason against that added exposure.

nodes.title: Easier for one-wage families to keep a mother at home
nodes.claim_html: Lower premiums would make it easier for some eligible one-wage families buying Marketplace coverage to keep a mother at home to care for children and teach the faith.

nodes.title: Tradition: a mother at home for religious upbringing
nodes.claim_html: Keeping a mother at home to raise children and pass on the faith is a practice valued in this tradition. Lowering its cost supports keeping it.

nodes.title: Tradition: no loss of all help for marrying above the cutoff
nodes.claim_html: For couples whose combined income crosses the cutoff, marrying no longer causes all help to disappear. Reducing that financial obstacle supports the traditional practice of marriage.

nodes.title: Less strain on churches and church giving
nodes.claim_html: Lower premiums would ease the strain on some pastoral families and small churches that help pay their insurance, and would leave some members more room to keep up customary giving.

nodes.title: Tradition: congregations’ worship and teaching
nodes.claim_html: Clergy, regular giving and worship are how congregations practice and pass on their faith. Easing pressure on them supports that continuity.

nodes.title: Christian health ministries under less strain
nodes.claim_html: Keeping more patients insured would ease unpaid bills and added demand for free care at Christian hospitals and church clinics.

nodes.title: Tradition: an established healing ministry
nodes.claim_html: Caring for the sick is an established Christian ministry. Easing strain on it helps those institutions carry it on.

nodes.title: Tradition: inherited family farms and rural life
nodes.claim_html: Keeping the land and work through which families pass on family and rural customs preserves an inherited way of life.

nodes.title: Tradition: the religious rule against abortion
nodes.claim_html: Continuing the religious rule against abortion gives a reason against making plans that cover it cheaper to enter.

nodes.title: Tradition: the rule against indirect support for abortion
nodes.claim_html: Preserving these religious bodies’ rule against indirect support gives a reason against added public payments to plans that cover abortion, whether or not abortion numbers rise.

nodes.title: Tradition: refusing payments that violate religious teaching
nodes.claim_html: Preserving the practice of refusing payments that violate religious teaching gives a reason against increasing the pressure to accept them.

nodes.title: Tradition: the inherited understanding of sex
nodes.claim_html: Maintaining this religious understanding of sex gives a reason against cheaper access to plans with transition benefits.

nodes.title: Tradition: Catholic teaching on conceiving children
nodes.claim_html: Preserving Catholic teaching on how spouses should conceive children gives a reason against cheaper access to IVF, which replaces the marital act.

nodes.title: Tradition: Catholic teaching on marriage and contraception
nodes.claim_html: Within Catholic traditionalism, maintaining this teaching about married sex gives a reason against widening access to contraception.

nodes.title: Tradition: Christian mutual aid
nodes.claim_html: Preserving the religious practice of sharing medical bills, giving and prayer gives a reason against a stronger financial incentive to leave it for insurance.

nodes.title: Tradition: a higher cost of marrying for some couples
nodes.claim_html: Maintaining the marriage tradition gives a reason against increasing the money some couples lose by marrying.
